Pseudonymize subject identifiers consistently across datasets

Source: R/anon_subject.R
anon_subject_ids.Rd

Replaces each subject's key (for example USUBJID) with a random pseudonym that is the same in every dataset, so the datasets can still be joined. Related identifier columns listed in also (for example SUBJID) are replaced with the pseudonym's number so they stay aligned with the key, and columns listed in key_cols that hold other subjects' keys (for example RSUBJID) are mapped through the same pseudonyms.

Usage

anon_subject_ids(
  data,
  key = "USUBJID",
  also = "SUBJID",
  key_cols = "RSUBJID",
  prefix = "SUBJ-",
  keep_secrets = FALSE,
  seed = NULL
)

Arguments

data

A data frame, a named list of data frames linked by key, or the result of an earlier step such as anon_subject_dates(). Datasets without the key column are returned unchanged.

key

Name of the subject identifier column.

also

Names of related identifier columns that hold one value per subject (default "SUBJID"). They are replaced with the pseudonym's number. Columns not present in a dataset are skipped.

key_cols

Names of columns that hold subject keys, possibly of other subjects (default "RSUBJID", as in SDTM RELSUB). Each value is replaced with that subject's pseudonym; values that are not a known key are removed with a warning.

prefix

Prefix for character pseudonyms, followed by a zero-padded number (e.g. "SUBJ-042"). Numeric keys get the number itself.

keep_secrets

Logical. If TRUE, keep the mapping from keys to pseudonyms; read it with anon_secrets(). Default FALSE: the mapping is not kept anywhere.

seed

Optional seed for the random assignment, for reproducible tests. Anyone with the seed and the original data can rebuild the mapping, so do not set it for data you share. The global random number state is restored afterwards.

Value

An object of class "anon_deid_step": a list with data (the transformed data, in the same form as the input), log (a tibble with step, dataset, variable, n_changed, n_removed and detail; the first row of each step records its settings; earlier steps are included when data was a step result), settings (a named list with each step's arguments, without the seed value) and secrets (NULL unless keep_secrets = TRUE here or in an earlier step). Saving the object (for example with saveRDS()) also saves its secrets.

Details

Pseudonyms are numbered in random order, and rows of each dataset are then sorted by the new key (keeping the order of rows within each subject), so neither the pseudonyms nor the row order reveal the order of the original keys. Column types and attributes such as variable labels are kept: character keys get character pseudonyms, numeric keys get numbers, factors stay factors. Value labels (haven labels), which describe the original values, are dropped from replaced columns. Missing and blank keys are left as they are. Values of also columns in rows without a key cannot be mapped and are removed (set to missing), with a warning. key, also and key_cols must not overlap.

A warning lists any other character or factor column (values or factor levels), in any dataset, that still contains original key values as whole values or as whole words inside text (checked for character keys that are not made only of digits, since numbers match many unrelated codes), and any dataset without key that has a column named like key, also or key_cols in any case. In datasets with key, a column named like one of them in another case (such as usubjid beside USUBJID) is not replaced and is named in a warning. Original values of also columns (such as SUBJID) elsewhere are not checked, because short numbers match many unrelated values. Missing values in also columns stay missing. In key, also and key_cols columns, haven user-defined missing values (na_values, na_range) become plain missing values and the codes are dropped, because a code can't be told apart from a real identifier.

Random numbers come from R's random number generator. If your script calls set.seed() before this step, anyone with the script and the data can reproduce the assignment.

Pseudonymized data remains personal data for anyone who holds the mapping or can re-identify subjects by other means; measure the remaining risk with anon_risk().

See also

anon_subject_dates(), anon_secrets(), anon_risk()

Examples

data <- list(
  dm = data.frame(USUBJID = c("01-701-1015", "01-701-1023"), SUBJID = c("1015", "1023")),
  vs = data.frame(USUBJID = c("01-701-1015", "01-701-1023"), VSSTRESN = c(70, 80))
)
result <- anon_subject_ids(data)
result$data
#> $dm
#>   USUBJID SUBJID
#> 1  SUBJ-1      1
#> 2  SUBJ-2      2
#> 
#> $vs
#>   USUBJID VSSTRESN
#> 1  SUBJ-1       70
#> 2  SUBJ-2       80
#>
